column1: In software architecture, what fundamentally distinguishes an 'architectural' decision from a routine engineering decision?
column2: The cost of reversal grows with time — architectural decisions calcify and become load-bearing for everything built on top, unlike cheaply revisable decisions like variable naming or data structure choice.

column1: What is Conway's Law, and why is it a causal mechanism rather than a suggestion?
column2: Any organization that designs a system produces a design mirroring its communication structure, because module ownership follows team ownership and interface friction follows team communication friction.

column1: What are the three categories of architectural constraints, and which is truly non-negotiable?
column2: Physical constraints (hardware limits like bandwidth/latency), organizational constraints (team structure), and business constraints (domain/compliance rules). Only physical constraints are truly non-negotiable; the others can be changed at a cost.

column1: What dependency direction rule defines a monolithic layered architecture?
column2: Unidirectional dependency flow: each layer depends only on abstractions from the layer below, never the reverse (higher levels operate in terms of services from lower levels).

column1: Why is a monolith's failure domain described as 'shared fate'?
column2: All layers share a single address space and process; a crash in any layer terminates the entire process, and a memory leak anywhere eventually exhausts the whole system.

column1: What are the three fundamental invariants of modular componentization?
column2: 1) Bounded context encapsulation (stable interface, free internal implementation), 2) Dependency directionality (acyclic dependency graphs/DAGs), 3) Interface stability under composition (substitutability preserves contracts).

column1: Why must module dependency graphs be acyclic (DAGs)?
column2: Cycles create semantic deadlock (A depends on B depends on C depends on A); a DAG enables topological sort, incremental compilation, independent testing, and bounded impact analysis.

column1: List four of the classic 'Fallacies of Distributed Computing.'
column2: Examples: the network is reliable; latency is zero; bandwidth is infinite; the network topology doesn't change; there is one administrator; transport cost is zero; the network is homogeneous.

column1: State the CAP theorem's three properties and its core impossibility result.
column2: Consistency (linearizability), Availability (bounded-time response from every non-failing node), Partition tolerance (operates despite message loss). In the presence of a partition (P), a system cannot simultaneously guarantee both C and A.

column1: Why does inter-data-center latency have a hard physical floor?
column2: The speed of light bounds propagation delay — e.g., ~6.7ms minimum round-trip for 1000km of fiber — before adding serialization, queuing, and handshake overhead.

column1: What single root operational pathology do monolith deployment issues (shared DB connections, memory leaks, coordinated deploys) stem from?
column2: Violation of the principle of isolation — components share runtime, deployment pipeline, transaction scope, and failure domain.

column1: Name three resilience patterns that limit blast radius in distributed systems, and what they each trade away.
column2: Bulkheads (partition thread pools to prevent resource exhaustion cascade), circuit breakers (halt retry storms to prevent cascading collapse), rate limiters (protect downstream dependencies). Each trades peak theoretical throughput for guaranteed operational headroom during failure.
